sections.normalized_html:
We are given the equation [MATH: \dfrac{1}{y^{2} + 12y + 36} = 9.]

First, we observe that the denominator is a perfect square trinomial: [MATH: y^{2} + 12y + 36 = (y + 6)^2] So, our equation becomes

[MATH: \dfrac{1}{(y + 6)^2} = 9.]

Now, we take the reciprocal of both sides: [MATH: (y + 6)^2 = \dfrac{1}{9}]

Next, we take the square root of both sides:

[MATH: sqrt((y + 6)^{2})|= sqrt((1)/(9)); y + 6|= ± (1)/(3)]

So, the possible values of [MATH: y + 6] are [MATH: -\dfrac13] and [MATH: \dfrac13.]

Among the listed options, only [MATH: \dfrac{1}{3}] is valid.

sections.normalized_html: What value of [MATH: n] satisfies the equation given below? [MATH: \dfrac{n^{2}}{n^{2} + 5n + 6} - \dfrac{2n}{n + 2} = -\,\dfrac{9}{n + 3}]
sections.readable_text:
What value of [MATH: n] satisfies the equation given below?
[MATH: \dfrac{n^{2}}{n^{2} + 5n + 6} - \dfrac{2n}{n + 2} = -\,\dfrac{9}{n + 3}]

sections.normalized_html:
First, we factor the denominators where possible. Note that [MATH: n^{2} + 5n + 6] factors as [MATH: (n + 2)(n + 3).]

So, we rewrite the expression as [MATH: \dfrac{n^{2}}{(n + 2)(n + 3)} - \dfrac{2n}{n + 2} = -\,\dfrac{9}{n + 3}.]

We now make the following observations:

  • The least common denominator of our equation is given by [MATH: \textrm{LCM}\big( n+2,\: n+3,\: (n+2)(n+3) \big) = (n+2)(n+3).]

  • The values [MATH: n=-2] and [MATH: n=-3] cannot be solutions to our equation. These values make at least one denominator in our original equation equal zero, and division by zero is undefined.

Now, multiplying both sides of the equation by the least common denominator, we can simplify it as follows: [MATH: ((n^{2})/((n + 2)(n + 3)) − (2n)/(n + 2)) ⋅ (n + 2)(n + 3)|= − (9)/(n + 3) ⋅ (n + 2)(n + 3); (n^{2})/((n + 2)(n + 3)) ⋅ (n + 2)(n + 3) − (2n)/(n + 2) ⋅ (n + 2)(n + 3)|= − (9)/(n + 3) ⋅ (n + 2)(n + 3); (n^{2})/((n + 2)(n + 3)) ⋅ (n + 2)(n + 3) − (2n)/(n + 2) ⋅ (n + 2)(n + 3)|= − (9)/(n + 3) ⋅ (n + 2)(n + 3); n^{2} − 2n(n + 3)|= − 9(n + 2).]

Now, we expand both sides, move all terms to the left-hand side, and factor the result to obtain [MATH: n^{2} − 2n^{2} − 6n|= − 9n − 18; − n^{2} + 3n + 18|= 0; n^{2} − 3n − 18|= 0; (n − 6)(n + 3)|= 0.]

By the zero-product property, the possible solutions are [MATH: n = 6] or [MATH: n = -3.]

However, [MATH: n = -3] is excluded because it makes the denominator zero. Therefore, the only valid solution is [MATH: n = 6.]
